FLEX (Flame Extinguishment Experiment) investigates the effectiveness of fire suppressants in microgravity and quantify the effect of different possible crew exploration atmospheres on fire suppression. There are five fuel samples. Experiment data records representing the fuel samples are:

FLEX – Calibration

FLEX - LCTF Calibration

FLEX - Radiometer Calibration

FLEX – HEP

FLEX – MeOH

These Experiment Data records are located on the “Data” tab within the FLEX investigation in PSI. When an experiment data record is selected, the “Scientific Data and Information” tab is opened. In the Experiment Data records “Raw Data”, “Analyzed Data”, “Raw Videos”, “Images” are organized by GMT data and/or gas mixture.

BASS-2 Engineering Requirements

General Requirements
Each Burning And Suppression of Solids-2 (BASS-2) solid fuel assembly is mounted inside the Experiment Assembly via a magnetic interface such that it can be installed and removed by the crew.
Solid fuel ignition will be done with a hot-wire Kanthol material igniter.
Nitrogen gas to be used from 0 to 500 SCCM N2. Instead of connecting the Experiment Assembly to the gas bottle it is connected via the GN2 hose to the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) gaseous nitrogen (GN2) supply interface.
3.2 mm normal length and 3.2 mm short length burner tubes will be manifested and used for BASS.
The Control Box will be modified to allow the fan flow adjustment to stop the fan when set to its minimum as a safety mechanism to extinguish flame.
Parameter Measurement
Measurement of the GN2 Flow rate, Fan Voltage, Co-Flow velocity, and flame radiation will be measured and overlaid on the video.
The data acquisition rate as measured by SPICE hardware is 4 Hz.
The measurement accuracy of ±10% was met by the SPICE hardware prior to its launch.

Spreadsheets folder has test matrix and fan calibration information.

Test Matrix explanation

Tabs in spreadsheet for each PI.

Subrata Bhattacharjee burned various thickness of very thin pmma films.

Paul Ferkul burned Nomex III and a candle to round out the BASS-I testing.

Fletcher Miller burned various thickness and widths of thick pmma slabs (one sided and two sided burns).

Sandra Olson burned three sizes of pmma rods (mostly clear), igniting the upstream end for a stagnation flame / concurrent flow geometry.

Carlos Fernandez-Pello burned three sizes of pmma rods (mostly black), igniting the downstream end for an opposed flow flame spread geometry.

James T’ien burned mostly SIBAL fabric (75/25 cotton/fiberglass blend). Also had 1 sample/2 tests with 4 cm pmma spherical section.

Columns in test matrix:

Date: actual date of experiment. Video display is one day later than actual date due to a leap year the on-board computer did not account for.

GMT- number is day of the year. ISS runs on Greenwich mean time, so their clock reads as GMT – Year – Day - time

doc_title: Laminar Smoke Points of Coflow Diffusion Flames in Microgravity (K. Dotson M.S. Thesis, UMD 2010)
text:
FLAMES

Keenan Thomas Dotson, M.S., 2009

Directed By: Assistant Professor, Peter B. Sunderland, 
Department of Fire Protection Engineering

Smoke points were measured in microgravity aboard the International Space Station 
(ISS) as part of the Smoke Points in Coflow Experiment (SPICE), and in normal 
gravity conditions. In microgravity conditions increasing the coflow velocity or 
decreasing the burner diameter increased the smoke point flame length. A simplified 
prediction of centerline jet velocity did not yield residence-time-based criticalities or 
data collapse. Simulation of non-reacting flows showed that the simplified centerline 
velocity prediction was able to predict velocity decay for only relatively weak 
coflows. An improved model may yield different results. In normal earth gravity 
coflow velocity exhibited mixed effects. For burner diameters of 0.41, 0.76, and 1.6 
mm, smoke points increased with increases of coflow velocity. For an unconfined 
coflow burner with a burner diameter of 13.7 mm smoke point length decreased with 
increasing coflow velocity for ethylene and propylene, while increasing for propane 
flames.

Smoke Point In Coflow Experiment 
“SPICE” 
Microgravity Science Glovebox 
Increment 19-20 (30 Day Report) 
Investigators: David Urban NASA GRC, Peter Sunderland: Univ. Maryland 
Project Scientist: Zengguang Yuan, National Center for Space Exploration Research 
Project Manager: Robert Hawersaat NASA GRC

I. Introduction

A. Hypothesis 
The hypothesis of the SPICE investi gation is that smoke point behavior 
will be observed for co-flowing flames and that it will show 
dependence on nozzle diameter and coflow velocity.

B. Objectives of Investigation 
The objective of the SPICE experiment is to find the laminar smoke-point 
properties of nonbuoyant jet diffusion flames (i.e., the properties of the 
largest laminar jet diffusion flames that do not emit soot) for several fuels 
under different nozzle diameter/ co-flow velocity configurations. 
Luminous flame shape measurements would also be made to verify 
models of the flame shapes under co-flow conditions.

C. Previous Mission Experience 
N/A

Memorandum SPICE-MEM-010

TO: Tibor Lorik, SPICE Project Lead, ZIN Technologies, Inc.

FROM: Kevin Magee, Project Engineer, ZIN Technologies, Inc.

SUBJECT: SPICE Flow Duct Velocity Measurements

DATE: July 6, 2009 
______________________________________________________________

This Memo addresses the SPICE flow duct velocity measurements, which were performed by Kevin 
Magee on the flight hardware from June 16-24, 2008. A hot wire anemometer probe was used to 
measure the air velocity at various points within the flow duct. This probe was passed into the duct 
through a special multi-piece top window with probe ports at the desired locations. Unused ports were 
taped shut on the inside and outside to prevent leakage and minimize flow disturbances. The window 
itself was assembled and sealed with Kapton tape around its perimeter.

The probe used was a TSI, Inc., Model 1261A miniature boundary layer probe (S/N# 012077) with a 
T1.5 (coated tungsten platinum) wire and a 56 ohm control resistor to give a 260oC operating 
temperature. Its calibration was performed in a free jet facility on April 28, 2006.

Study Public Release Date: 18-Sep-2024
Study File Name: s_PSI-107.txt
Comment[Approach]: The experimental setup in the microgravity science glovebox consisted of an apparatus with a flow duct with integrated nozzles, cameras, and fuel delivery systems. Fuels tested included methane, ethylene, propane, propylene, and propylene mixtures. Each flame was ignited in a controlled co-flow air environment, with burner diameters of 0.41 mm, 0.76 mm, and 1.6 mm and co-flow velocities ranging from 5.4 cm/s to 65 cm/s. Fuel flow rates were adjusted to identify the smoke point, marked by the flame's transition to emitting soot. Data such as flame lengths were recorded using still and video cameras. Measurements included flame height, radiative heat losses, and co-flow air velocity distributions.
